title: In the Beginning
subtitle: Genesis in Poems & Pictures
beforeYouBegin:
Genesis runs from the first light to a coffin in Egypt: a garden, a flood, a family that God promises to bless, and the long, tangled story of how he keeps that promise through liars, wrestlers, and brothers who sold their brother.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. It doesn't cover every chapter; it stops at the moments that carry the story.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open Genesis alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Part One · In the Beginning
parts.epigraph: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

parts.title: Part Two · The Friend of God
parts.epigraph: Go to the land that I will show you.

parts.title: Part Three · Wrestling
parts.epigraph: Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel

parts.title: Part Four · God Meant It for Good
parts.epigraph: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good

paintings.title: let there be
paintings.poem:
before anything,
a voice
over dark water.
no struggle.
no battle with the deep.
just a sentence—
and light
did what it was told,
and has been doing it
every morning since.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “let there be” (Genesis 1:1-3)—where the poem notes, “and has been doing it every morning since”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: very good
paintings.poem:
six times he stepped back
and said: good.
the light. the land.
the seas and the seeds.
the lights in the sky.
the swimmers and the fliers.
the cattle and the creeping things.
and at the end,
looking at all of it,
with us in it:
very good.
remember that
on the days
you forget it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “very good” (Genesis 1:31)—where the poem notes, “on the days you forget it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the gallery
paintings.poem:
every face you pass today
was made to look like someone.
not like a king.
not like a statue in a temple.
like God.
the beggar and the boss,
the man and the woman,
the neighbor you avoid—
you are walking
through a gallery
of his image.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the gallery” (Genesis 1:27)—where the poem notes, “through a gallery of his image”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the seventh day
paintings.poem:
he finished,
and then he stopped.
not because he was tired.
because rest
was part of the making.
the first thing God called holy
wasn't a place.
it was a day
with nothing to do.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (Genesis 2:1-3)?

paintings.title: dust and breath
paintings.poem:
his name is a play on words:
Adam,
from adamah,
the ground.
we are dirt
that God leaned close to
and breathed on.
so be humble—
you're dust.
and be amazed—
you're breathed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “dust and breath” (Genesis 2:7)—where the poem notes, “and be amazed— you're breathed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not good
paintings.poem:
everything was good,
until God noticed
one thing that wasn't.
not sin. not yet.
just a man
with no one beside him.
the first "not good"
in the Bible
is loneliness.
God took it seriously.
so should we.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not good” (Genesis 2:18)—where the poem notes, “God took it seriously. so should we”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: where are you?
paintings.poem:
he knew where they were.
the question wasn't for him.
it was for them—
crouched among the trees,
sewing leaves,
ashamed of their own skin.
where are you?
not a hunter's shout.
a father's call
at evening,
walking the garden
the way he always did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “where are you?” (Genesis 3:8-9)—where the poem notes, “walking the garden the way he always did”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: clothed
paintings.poem:
there were consequences—
thorns, sweat,
the long road out.
but before they left,
God knelt
and made them clothes.
theirfig leaves
weren't enough.
his mercy
was.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “clothed” (Genesis 3:21)—where the poem notes, “his mercy was”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: keeper
paintings.poem:
the first question was:
where are you?
the second:
where is your brother?
Cain shrugged.
am I supposed to keep track of him?
yes.
that is exactly
what you were for.
and the ground itself
would not stay quiet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “keeper” (Genesis 4:9-10)—where the poem notes, “and the ground itself would not stay quiet”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: one green leaf
paintings.poem:
the first time, she came back
with nothing.
the second time, at evening,
a leaf.
fresh. green.
torn from a living tree.
that's all.
not the end of the flood—
proof that it was ending.
sometimes hope
is one small green thing
carried a long way.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “one green leaf” (Genesis 8:6-11)—where the poem notes, “is one small green thing carried a long way”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the bow in the cloud
paintings.poem:
a warrior's bow,
hung up
in the clouds.
and God said:
when I see it,
I will remember.
not you—
I.
the promise doesn't depend
on your memory.
it hangs on his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the bow in the cloud” (Genesis 9:13-15)—where the poem notes, “on your memory. it hangs on his”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a name for ourselves
paintings.poem:
come, let's build.
let's reach the sky.
let's make a name—
the oldest plan in the world.
they wanted height.
God wanted them spread across the earth.
a chapter later,
he calls one man
and says:
I will make your name great.
the name you build
falls.
the name you're given
stands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:1-9)—where the poem notes, “the name you're given stands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: go
paintings.poem:
leave.
your country.
your family.
your father's house.
go.
where?
I'll show you.
no map,
only a voice—
and a seventy- five-year-old man
packs his tents.
faith often starts
with not knowing
where.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “go” (Genesis 12:1-4)—where the poem notes, “with not knowing where”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: count them
paintings.poem:
he was old,
and had no son,
and God took him outside
and said: look up.
count them.
he couldn't.
that was the point.
and he believed—
and God counted that
as righteousness.
the first thing faith does
is step outside
and look up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “count them” (Genesis 15:5-6)—where the poem notes, “is step outside and look up”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the God who sees
paintings.poem:
Hagar—
a slave, a foreigner,
pregnant, mistreated,
run away into the desert.
nobody's first choice.
and God found her by a spring
and called her by name.
and she gave God a name
no one had given him before:
the God who sees.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the God who sees” (Genesis 16:7-13)—where the poem notes, “no one had given him before: the God who sees”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: too hard
paintings.poem:
she laughed
inside the tent,
the way you laugh
at a promise that's come too late.
old.
worn out.
done hoping.
and a voice outside asked:
is anything too hard for the Lord?
that question is still standing
in the doorway
of every tent
where someone stopped hoping.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “too hard” (Genesis 18:10-14)—where the poem notes, “of every tent where someone stopped hoping”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: laughter
paintings.poem:
she named him Laughter—
Isaac.
the same laugh
that once meant
I don't believe it
now means
I can't believe it.
God doesn't scold her.
he gives her a son
and a better reason
to laugh.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “laughter” (Genesis 21:1-7)—where the poem notes, “and a better reason to laugh”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the Lord will provide
paintings.poem:
where is the lamb, father?
God will provide, my son.
and they walked on,
the two of them together,
up the mountain.
this is the hardest chapter
in the book,
and the story tells it
in a hush.
but it ends
with a ram in the thicket
and a new name for the mountain:
the Lord will provide.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the Lord will provide” (Genesis 22:7-14)—where the poem notes, “and a new name for the mountain: the Lord will provide”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the camels too
paintings.poem:
a stranger asked for a drink.
she gave it.
then she said:
I'll water your camels too—
ten thirsty camels,
jar after jar
from the well.
the servant had prayed for a sign.
he got a young woman
who did more
than she was asked.
that is often
how God answers:
through someone's
generous hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of Genesis 24:15-20?

paintings.title: full of years
paintings.poem:
he left home at seventy- five
on a promise.
he did not see
the nation,
the land,
the stars made good.
he saw one son,
a burial cave,
and a lifetime of God
keeping his word
a little at a time.
and he died
full of years.
not empty.
full.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “full of years” (Genesis 25:7-8)—where the poem notes, “not empty. full”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: red stew
paintings.poem:
he came in starving
and traded his future
for a bowl of red stew.
it tasted good.
it was gone in minutes.
don't laugh at Esau too quickly.
we all have a bowl
we'd sell tomorrow
for tonight.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “red stew” (Genesis 25:29-34)—where the poem notes, “we'd sell tomorrow for tonight”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the stairway
paintings.poem:
he was running
from a brother he had cheated,
sleeping on the ground
with a stone for a pillow.
and heaven
came down a stairway
to meet him there.
not because he had earned it.
because God had promised,
and does not wait
for us to deserve it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Genesis 28:10-15 (“and does not wait for us to deserve it”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: I didn't know it
paintings.poem:
God was here,
and I didn't know it.
maybe the most honest sentence
anyone ever said
waking up.
so he set up the stone
and poured oil on it
to remember:
the lonely place,
the hard ground,
the night I ran—
God was here.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “I didn't know it” (Genesis 28:16-18)—where the poem notes, “the night I ran— God was here”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a few days
paintings.poem:
seven years of work
for Rachel.
and the book says
they went by
like a few days.
love does strange things
to the clock.
the story after this
is not simple.
the book won't pretend it is.
but this line
is true.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a few days” (Genesis 29:18-20)—where the poem notes, “but this line is true”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: until the day breaks
paintings.poem:
alone at the river,
at night,
someone takes hold of him,
and he fights back
till dawn.
he's wrestled all his life—
his brother, his father,
his uncle, his fear.
now he wrestles God
and won't let go:
not until you bless me.
it is the most Jacob thing
he ever said,
and the most faithful.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Genesis 32:24-26?

paintings.title: the limp
paintings.poem:
he walked away
blessed
and limping.
a new name.
a new way of walking.
some blessings
come with a limp,
so you never forget
who you met
by the river.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the limp” (Genesis 32:30-31)—where the poem notes, “who you met by the river”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: Esau ran
paintings.poem:
twenty years of dread.
four hundred men coming.
gifts sent ahead in waves.
and then—
Esau ran.
not to fight.
to hold him.
the thing you feared most
may be running toward you
with open arms.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Genesis 33:1-4?

paintings.title: the coat
paintings.poem:
a father's favorite,
and everyone knew it.
the coat said so
every time he wore it.
love is good.
favoritism
tears a family
like cloth.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the coat” (Genesis 37:3-4)—where the poem notes, “tears a family like cloth”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the empty pit
paintings.poem:
no water in it.
no way out.
seventeen,
and his brothers sit down to eat
on the rim.
this is where
the dream seems to die.
it doesn't.
it is going down
the way seeds go down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the empty pit” (Genesis 37:23-25)—where the poem notes, “it is going down the way seeds go down”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the refrain
paintings.poem:
sold as a slave:
the Lord was with Joseph.
falsely accused:
the Lord was with Joseph.
thrown in prison:
the Lord was with Joseph.
the chapter keeps saying it,
like a drumbeat
under the worst years of his life.
the circumstances change.
the refrain
doesn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the refrain” (Genesis 39:2-23)—where the poem notes, “the refrain doesn't”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: forgotten
paintings.poem:
remember me, Joseph said,
when it goes well for you.
and it went well for him.
and he forgot.
two more years
in the dark.
if you've been forgotten
by someone who promised,
you are not forgotten
by the One who did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “forgotten” (Genesis 40:14-23)—where the poem notes, “you are not forgotten by the One who did”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not in me
paintings.poem:
shaved, dressed,
pulled from the prison,
he stands before the king of Egypt,
who says:
I hear you can interpret dreams.
it's his big chance.
and his first words are:
it isn't in me.
the most useful people God has
are the ones
who know
where the gift came from.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not in me” (Genesis 41:14-16)—where the poem notes, “who know where the gift came from”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: faces to the earth
paintings.poem:
they came for grain
and bowed to the governor
with their faces in the dust.
they didn't know him.
he knew them.
the dream from the field,
the sheaves bowing down—
come true
in a way
nobody wanted anymore.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “faces to the earth” (Genesis 42:6-8)—where the poem notes, “in a way nobody wanted anymore”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: instead of the boy
paintings.poem:
Judah—
the brother who once said
let's sell him—
now says:
take me instead.
let the boy go home.
it would kill our father.
that's how Joseph knew
they had changed.
a man who once sold a brother
now offers himself
for one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “instead of the boy” (Genesis 44:30-34)—where the poem notes, “now offers himself for one”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: come near
paintings.poem:
he sent everyone out
and wept so loud
the Egyptians heard it.
I am Joseph.
and they couldn't speak.
then the gentlest words
in the whole long story:
come near to me.
please.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come near” (Genesis 45:1-4)—where the poem notes, “come near to me. please”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: sent
paintings.poem:
don't be angry with yourselves,
he said.
you sold me.
God sent me.
both are true.
he doesn't pretend
the first one didn't happen.
he just refuses
to let it be
the whole story.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “sent” (Genesis 45:5-8)—where the poem notes, “to let it be the whole story”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the wagons
paintings.poem:
Joseph is alive, they said,
and the old man
didn't believe them.
then he saw the wagons.
sometimes it isn't the words
that raise a heart.
it's the wagons—
proof you can touch
that someone
is coming to carry you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the wagons” (Genesis 45:25-28)—where the poem notes, “that someone is coming to carry you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a good while
paintings.poem:
twenty-two years.
a chariot racing up from Egypt,
an old man leaning on his staff,
and the book, usually so brisk,
slows down:
he wept on his neck
a good while.
some reunions
you don't hurry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a good while” (Genesis 46:28-30)—where the poem notes, “some reunions you don't hurry”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: underneath
paintings.poem:
you meant it for evil.
God meant it for good.
not: it wasn't evil.
not: it didn't hurt.
but underneath the worst thing
anyone ever did to him,
another hand
was working
the whole time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “underneath” (Genesis 50:15-21)—where the poem notes, “was working the whole time”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the road home
paintings.poem:
the book that began
with light and a garden
ends
with a coffin in Egypt.
but not with despair.
Joseph's last words:
God will surely come for you.
take my bones with you
when you go.
Genesis ends
with a promise,
and bones ready
for the road home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the road home” (Genesis 50:24-26)—where the poem notes, “and bones ready for the road home”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
